item.title: BAHCC1 Drives Smooth Muscle Plasticity and Neointima via Epigenetic Repression.
item.author: Tang R, Huang Y, Shirasu T, Li J, Webb A, Zheng K, Shen C, Guo Y, Auguste G, Hart P, Murach M, Zhou X, Ma J, Kent KC, Wang GG, Yang J, Miller CL, Martin KA, Guo LW.
item.description:
Background Vascular smooth muscle cell (SMC) phenotypic plasticity drives neointimal hyperplasia (IH) and contributes to atherosclerosis. Epigenetic mechanisms have been implicated in SMC plasticity, but the roles of epigenetic reader proteins are poorly understood. BAHCC1 (bromo adjacent homology domain coiled-coil 1) is a newly identified reader of the gene-repression histone mark histone-3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3). Its role in vascular remodeling is unknown. Methods We investigated BAHCC1 in human restenotic and atherosclerotic arteries and in rat and mouse arterial injury models using BAHCC1 silencing, SMC-specific deletion, and an H3K27me3-binding-deficient knock-in mutation. Mechanistic studies in human aortic SMCs integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling, protein-interaction assays, and single-guide RNA-dCas9-based epigenetic editing. item.title: VSMC DDR1 Mechanosensation Aggravates Atherosclerosis via Paracrine Signaling.
item.author: Zhou S, Chu X, Zhang J, Zhang J, Xu Y, Fan L, Liang Z, Shen Y, Yao W, Chen Z, Fu Y, Zhang T, Zhou J.
item.description:
Background Chronic kidney disease (CKD) increases cardiovascular risk and is linked to arterial stiffening and atherosclerosis. How stiffness promotes atherogenesis remains unclear. DDR1 (discoidin domain receptor 1), a mechanosensory tyrosine kinase receptor, has been implicated in force-regulated arterial remodeling. We investigated whether DDR1-mediated mechanosensation links arterial stiffness to vascular smooth muscle cell (SMC)-endothelial paracrine communication in CKD-related atherosclerosis. Methods Single-cell RNA sequencing, secretome proteomics, and bulk RNA sequencing were integrated with stiffness-controlled models, endothelial assays, and a CKD-hyperlipidemia mouse model. SMC-specific Ddr1 deletion and a DDR1 dephosphorylation-targeting chimera (DEPTAC) were evaluated in vivo. item.author: Emig R, Robbe Z, Kley C, Smolgovsky S, Bayer AL, Travers J, Blanton RM, McKinsey T, Black LD, Alcaide P.
item.description:
Background Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a major clinical challenge characterized by diastolic dysfunction. Left ventricular stiffening and inflammation are hallmarks of HFpEF, yet the contribution of ECM (extracellular matrix) stiffness and the immune-stromal mechanisms driving ECM stiffening in cardiometabolic HFpEF remain poorly understood. Methods We used the murine 2-hit model of cardiometabolic HFpEF, in which the combination of high-fat diet and hypertension induced by L-nitro-arginine-methyl ester causes diastolic dysfunction. We evaluated diastolic function by echocardiography and ECM mechanics by uniaxial tensile testing of decellularized cardiac tissue. item.title: Glutaminolysis Shapes Cardiac Resilience to Stress via Mitochondrial Glutathione.
item.author: Wang X, Zhou J, Bai H, Wei Z, Su L, Xing C, Wu G, Li M, An J, Zhang P, Zhang Y, Ding S, Zhang X, Ren J, Gao F, Li J.
item.description:
Background Cardiac reserve is a strong predictor of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, yet the metabolic mechanisms that enable the heart to mount an adaptive response to stress remain poorly understood. In this study, we sought to dissect the specific role of glutaminolysis, a key anaplerotic and redox-supporting pathway, in regulating cardiac reserve. Methods Cardiac reserve was assessed by echocardiography under β-adrenergic stimulation in mice with cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of glutaminase and in wild-type controls. Stable isotope tracing with [U- 13 C] glutamine was performed in Langendorff-perfused hearts. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of acute glutamine supplementation in healthy volunteers was conducted to evaluate translational relevance (ChiCTR2400082676). item.description:
Background Haploinsufficiency of the RNA splicing regulator RBFOX2 has been linked to congenital heart disease, including hypoplastic left heart syndrome, yet its pathogenic mechanisms remain unresolved. Methods Human induced pluripotent stem cells heterozygous or null for RBFOX2 were created and their cardiomyocyte (CM) derivatives were characterized in monolayer culture and engineered heart tissues. In addition to cellular phenotyping, molecular profiling by RNA sequencing and enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation sequencing was performed to detect changes in gene expression, exon usage, and RBFOX2 (RNA-binding fox-1 homolog 2) binding. These data sets were integrated to identify RBFOX2-bound RNAs with altered expression and splicing and to compare them with publicly available data sets from progressive CM differentiation time points. item.title: Maternal Microvascular Calcium Sparks Are Reduced in Preeclampsia.
item.author: Parnell LC, Tierney AL, Cottrell EC, Pritchard HAT, Smith MN, Krakowiak K, Unwin RD, Gurney AM, Myers JE, Greenstein A, Worton SA.
item.description:
Background Maternal microvascular dysfunction is a hallmark of the hypertensive pregnancy disorder preeclampsia, but the mechanism(s) have not been fully defined. Within vascular smooth muscle cells, the principal pressure-induced vasodilatory pathway depends on localized Ca 2+ -release events from the sarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine receptors (Ca 2+ sparks), which stimulate BK Ca (large-conductance Ca 2+ -activated potassium channels) to cause spontaneous transient outward currents and vasorelaxation. Here, the Ca 2+ sparks-BK Ca axis is assessed in preeclampsia for the first time. Methods Pressurized omental resistance arteries from normotensive pregnant women and women with preeclampsia were imaged by high-speed spinning-disk laser confocal microscopy to assess Ca 2+ sparks (20-110 mm Hg) and caffeine-evoked Ca 2+ release (10 mmol/L; 80 mm Hg). item.description:
Background Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a disease of neonatal lung development that is linked to impaired pulmonary vascularization, dysregulated TGF-β (transforming growth factor-β) signaling, and the accumulation of senescent cells. Despite the established role of TGF-β signaling in promoting vascular remodeling and suppressing the senolytic activity of natural killer (NK) cells, the contribution of NK cell TGF-β signaling to postnatal lung patterning and the pathogenesis of BPD remains unclear. item.title: CCR2-Dependent Myeloid Cell Recruitment Links Post-MI Heart Failure to Pulmonary Hypertension.
item.author: Gillan JL, Kamp J, Kucherenko MM, Winkler A, Funk-Hilsdorf TC, Jaeschke L, Hegemann N, Bintig W, Wirth EK, Simmons S, Momin N, Foris V, Kovacs G, Kuebler WM, Knosalla C, Grune J.
item.description:
Background Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (PH-LHD) is a common complication of myocardial infarction (MI) and heart failure (HF). Myeloid inflammation is a major hallmark of both the local cardiac and systemic post-MI response, with resident and recruited monocyte-derived macrophages orchestrating each step of the ensuing inflammatory cascade, from clearance of dead cardiomyocytes to scar tissue formation. Similarly, myeloid inflammation is a key feature of the PH lung, driving remodeling of small pulmonary vessels. We thus hypothesized that MI-induced systemic myeloid inflammation contributes directly to the development of PH-LHD. item.description:
Background Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a debilitating disease with a poor prognosis. However, only a limited number of palliative interventions are currently available. To address this unmet need, it is essential to understand the molecular causes of PAH by identifying unique disease-associated populations and their key molecular regulators during disease progression. Methods We constructed a single-cell multiome data set at 4 distinct time points during the pathogenesis of pulmonary hypertension (PH) using endothelial cells isolated from the Sugen5416/hypoxia rat model. We assessed the conservation of novel disease-associated endothelial cells by reanalyzing previously reported single-cell RNA sequencing data from human patients with PAH.
